title: When the disaster is real and the link isn’t
body_md:
## A real flood, a false address

The photograph is genuine: a street under brown water, a family on a roof. Everyone you know has shared it. Underneath sits a wallet address that belongs to someone who was never on that street. A disaster can be real while the payment link is false.

Three things can come apart: the cause, the person collecting and the place the money lands. An imitator borrows a charity’s name and photographs. A fundraiser announces a collection for a named family that never agreed to it. Even an honest crowdfunding organizer may not be the beneficiary. The urge to act at once is a good one, and it eats the minutes you would need to trace the recipient. A harrowing picture or a friend’s repost is not verification.

### Start from the name, not the link

Begin with the exact legal name of the charity, or the named person the money is for. Find its site through a reference you already trust or an official registry, and give by the route that site publishes. With crowdfunding, learn who the organizer is, who the beneficiary is and what the platform’s rules say; if you cannot confirm the organizer will pass the money on, give to a charity directly. Registration and tax treatment vary by country. In the US, the FTC suggests checking state registration and, separately, IRS tax-exempt status where deductibility matters. A listing still cannot vouch for every campaign that uses the name.

### How they ask you to pay

The payment method tells you something too. The FTC warns, in its US context, that a fundraiser who will take only cryptocurrency, gift cards, wires or payment apps is showing a strong danger sign. A genuine charity, though, may offer many ways to give, digital ones included, so no single method works as a test of honesty. HTTPS encrypts a donation form and says nothing about whose it is. Pause briefly to verify; no universal 24-hour wait exists. Save the receipt and check whether you switched on a recurring donation by accident. If you paid a doubtful collector, ask your payment provider promptly what can be done and report it to the proper local authority. Getting the money back is not certain.

widget_config.goal: Find out who actually receives the money, and still give to the cause you care about.
widget_config.today_action: Choose a cause you support, find its official donation page on your own and bookmark it. The next appeal can then be checked against it.
widget_config.scope: The FTC guidance covers US charities, payment methods and tax status; other countries keep different registries and protections. The examples are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: FTC: Before Giving to a Charity
sources.scope: US guidance on charities, fundraisers and payment methods. Registration rules differ elsewhere.

sources.title: FTC: What To Do if You Were Scammed
sources.scope: US steps through your payment provider and your accounts. It promises no recovery.

blocks.title: The flood post with a private wallet
blocks.situation: A post is making the rounds with real photographs of a flood and the name of a well-known aid group. It asks donors to send money to a personal crypto wallet that appears nowhere but in the post.
blocks.analysis: Real photos and a real flood do nothing to validate that wallet. Open the group’s official site yourself and give through the channel it publishes. If the post’s campaign cannot be matched there, send nothing to it.

blocks.title: Supplies leaving this afternoon
blocks.situation: A registered local relief group announces a supply run for this afternoon. You find its site on your own: it names the project and the exact legal entity, offers a card donation form and publishes a contact. When you ask the organizer questions, the answers stay consistent.
blocks.analysis: Urgency alone does not make an appeal fraudulent. Confirm the entity and the recipient through your own country’s system, read what the project is, and use the official payment route. Once you are satisfied you can give straight away; there is no waiting period to serve.

blocks.title: Where the money goes
blocks.setup: An invented evening: a storm has hit the coast and you want to help. A friend forwards a moving post that links to `coast-help.example`.

steps.prompt: The post names a well-known charity. How do you reach it?

choices.text: Click the link, because your friend sent it.
choices.consequence: Your friend may have passed on a link nobody checked.

choices.text: Find the charity’s official site or registry entry yourself.
choices.consequence: You have separated the charity from the URL you were handed.
choices.explanation: A real name is easy to borrow.

steps.prompt: Back at your friend’s link, the page is a crowdfunding appeal, not the charity’s own site. What has to be clear?

choices.text: Who organizes it, who receives the money and how the transfer to the cause is confirmed.
choices.consequence: You can judge whether this route will reach the people you mean to help.
choices.explanation: The organizer and the beneficiary can be different people.

choices.text: Only how moving the photo is.
choices.consequence: Where the payment lands is still unknown.
choices.explanation: Emotion is no record of a transfer.

steps.prompt: Then your phone rings. A caller collecting for the same cause says only gift cards will arrive in time. What next?

choices.text: Read the gift-card codes out over the phone.
choices.consequence: The codes can be spent the moment you have said them.
choices.explanation: The codes go to the caller; the charity never sees them.

choices.text: Decline, and give through the route you verified yourself.
choices.consequence: You can still support the cause without the forced payment method.
choices.explanation: A gift-card-only demand is a strong warning sign.

steps.prompt: Last checkpoint, whichever way you went: through a verified route, by reading out gift-card codes, or by paying nothing. What follow-up helps?

choices.text: Keep receipts, any gift cards and messages, check charges and recurring settings, and call the gift-card company now if codes went out.
choices.consequence: You can spot a charge you did not intend and explain a payment or lost codes. The company can lay out the options, but getting the money back is uncertain.
choices.explanation: Records pay off even when the cause is real; the FTC advises calling the gift-card company quickly if a scammer got the codes.

choices.text: Delete the records and ignore later account activity.
choices.consequence: You could miss another charge, or lose the proof of a payment or of exposed codes.
choices.explanation: Even an honest donation can need correcting, and lost gift-card codes call for quick action.

blocks.debrief: You can help quickly once you have traced the legal recipient and the payment path. A real crisis does not vouch for any particular post. Go back and take the other fork wherever you want to see what it costs.

questions.prompt: A friend shares a photo of real damage along with a wallet address. What does the photo prove?

choices.text: That the wallet belongs to the victims.
choices.explanation: A photo cannot show who owns a wallet.

choices.text: The event may be real; nothing links the wallet to the relief effort.
choices.explanation: Where a photo came from and where the money goes are separate questions.

questions.prompt: A registered charity is running an urgent drive. Must you wait 24 hours before giving?

choices.text: No: verify independently, then give when you are ready.
choices.explanation: The safeguard is the verification, not a fixed delay.

choices.text: Yes: every urgent appeal is a fraud until tomorrow.
choices.explanation: Real emergencies exist, and so does honest rapid response.

questions.prompt: A US charity appears on a tax-exempt list. What is left to check?

choices.text: Nothing; any link carrying its name is safe.
choices.explanation: A listing cannot authenticate a link on social media.

choices.text: That this campaign and this payment destination really belong to it.
choices.explanation: Imitators borrow the names of real charities.
